Model validation19 Nov 2026

Testing Zero-G Firewall on an unseen regime

The FLEX table contains repeat experiments. Keeping related runs together changes what the model’s error can tell us.

Martin Stefanov

A model can appear to generalize when its test set contains variations of experiments it has already seen. Zero-G Firewall’s FLEX model is a useful case. Its target is the measured burning-rate constant of a liquid droplet, expressed in mm²/s in the project. Several runs share the same fuel, pressure band and surrounding gas composition.

Decide what a new case means

The project’s copy of the PSI-69 FLEX experimental table contains 274 rows. Sixteen have no target value and one has no ambient pressure, leaving 257 usable runs. The training pipeline assigns them to 78 regimes using the fuel, nominal pressure band, diluent and rounded gas fractions. Those inputs are known before the result of a burn is observed.

Five-fold grouped validation keeps each regime in a single outer fold. The exported row-by-row evaluation confirms that all 78 groups satisfy that rule. A held-out prediction therefore answers a concrete question about a regime left out during fitting, within the two fuels and the facility represented in the data.

Read the number for the selection procedure

Procedure Mean absolute error (mm²/s) R²
Training median for the same fuel 0.1027 0.050
Physics-informed ridge candidate 0.0477 0.707
Ridge family chosen inside each training fold 0.0485 0.703

The final exported model uses the physics-informed ridge variant. The project also records what happens when the choice between two ridge families is made afresh inside each outer training fold. That nested result, 0.0485 mm²/s, includes the cost of making the selection on new data. It is the number to use when describing the selection procedure.

Decide when to withhold a prediction

The browser checks the query before evaluating the coefficients. The model covers methanol and heptane droplets in free fall without forced flow. Even a query within the ranges for its fuel must match a known regime and be close enough to a recorded run. A solid material or a lunar-gravity case returns a reason for abstaining. This keeps an estimate of a droplet property tied to the experiment that gives the number meaning.
